title: “Souper” paper dress
lede: A promotional paper dress from Campbell’s Soup, printed with rows of soup-can labels after Andy Warhol’s Campbell’s Soup Cans.
summary: A shift dress printed with a grid of red and white Campbell’s labels. Campbell’s Soup, USA, 1967.

evidence.note: Downloaded and inspected the V&A image of its copy, T.66-2016 (1200 × 1600 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.

styles.note: Pop art’s packaging grid returned to commerce: the soup label repeated in rows as a textile print. Partial fit: it has no dots or comic devices.

context: The V&A describes a short sleeveless dress of bonded-fibre “paper”, made in the USA in 1967 and produced to promote Campbell’s vegetable soup, after Andy Warhol’s soup cans of 1962. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1330466/).
The V&A notes that paper dresses were a brief sensation from 1966 to 1968, and that many were free gifts that promoted consumer products. [V&A](https://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O1330466/).
The painting series it follows is [Campbell’s Soup Cans](ref:warhol-campbells-soup-cans-1962).
observed: The dress is printed with four rows of soup-can labels in a regular grid; the labels are cut off at the side seams.
Each label has a red top half with the white script “Campbell’s” and a white bottom half with “SOUP” in black slab-serif capitals.
A gold medallion sits on the line between red and white; a row of small gold fleurs-de-lis runs along the bottom of each label.
Thin black vertical lines separate the labels.
Two gold stripes run along the hem. The neckline and armholes are bound in black.
interpretation: The dress closes the loop between packaging and Pop: a painter’s grid of labels becomes a product’s own promotion.
Repetition of one unit in a strict grid is a Pop layout device as important as the comic panel.
borrow: Repeat one product unit in a strict grid of cells separated by thin black rules.
Crop the grid at the edges of the container so that it reads as an endless pattern.

rights.statement: No image is stored. The label design is a Campbell’s trademark, and the print follows Andy Warhol’s work; rights are unverified.
